lessons.title: Write and Evaluate Algebraic Expressions
lessons.objective: I can write an algebraic expression for a real situation and evaluate it for a given value of the variable.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my expression using the words variable, term, coefficient, constant, substitute, and evaluate.

concept.heading: How do we turn words into an expression?
concept.intro: An algebraic expression uses numbers, a variable (a letter for an unknown number), and operations. We read a word phrase and write it with math symbols.
concept.keyIdea: Writing & Evaluating Algebraic Expressions. 1. Define the variable to represent the unknown quantity. 2. Translate mathematical phrases into operations, coefficients, and constants. 3. Evaluate by substituting given numerical values for the variable

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Tickets cost $12 each, plus a flat $50 venue fee. Let t be the number of tickets.
"$12 each ticket" means 12 times t, which I write as 12t.
The flat fee $50 is added once, so I add 50.
I put them together: total revenue = 12t + 50.
linesEs: Los boletos cuestan $12 cada uno, más una cuota fija de $50 por el lugar. Sea t el número de boletos.
«$12 por cada boleto» significa 12 por t, que escribo como 12t.
La cuota fija de $50 se suma una sola vez, así que sumo 50.

together.title: Let's write one together
lines: The field day committee orders one $4.25 item for each student, plus a one-time $23.50 shipping fee. The number of students is unknown.
Let s stand for the number of students. “$4.25 for each student” means 4.25 times s, written 4.25s.
The shipping fee does not depend on how many students there are, so it is a constant that is added once: 4.25s + 23.50.
The expression 4.25s + 23.50 has two terms: 4.25s, whose coefficient is 4.25, and the constant 23.50.
linesEs: El comité del día de campo pide un artículo de $4.25 para cada estudiante, más una cuota única de envío de $23.50. No se sabe cuántos estudiantes hay.
Sea s el número de estudiantes. «$4.25 por cada estudiante» significa 4.25 por s, escrito 4.25s.
La cuota de envío no depende de cuántos estudiantes haya, así que es una constante que se suma una vez: 4.25s + 23.50.
La expresión 4.25s + 23.50 tiene dos términos: 4.25s, cuyo coeficiente es 4.25, y la constante 23.50.

vocabulary.definition: Translate words or a situation into numbers, variables, and operation symbols.
vocabulary.example: Five more than n becomes n + 5.

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for a number that is unknown or can change.
vocabulary.example: In 5t + 20, t could be hours worked — if t = 3, the expression equals 35; if t = 8, it equals 60

vocabulary.definition: A math phrase that has at least one letter.
vocabulary.example: 3n + 7 means 'triple a number, then add 7' — it has a variable (n), a coefficient (3), and a constant (7)

vocabulary.definition: The number in front of a letter, like the 3 in 3x.
vocabulary.example: In 8x, the coefficient 8 means '8 groups of x' — if x = 3, then 8x = 8 × 3 = 24

vocabulary.definition: A fixed number in an expression or equation that does not change.
vocabulary.example: In 3n + 7, the 7 never changes no matter what n is — like a flat fee that stays the same

vocabulary.definition: Terms with the same letter raised to the same power, like 2x and 5x.
vocabulary.example: 4x + 2x = 6x (like terms, same variable); but 4x + 2y cannot be combined (different variables)

vocabulary.definition: To replace a variable with a given number before working out the value.
To find what an expression is worth once every variable has a number, following the order of operations.
One part of an expression, separated from the others by + or −.
vocabulary.example: In 14m + 35, the terms are 14m and 35.

lessons.title: Identify Equivalent Algebraic Expressions
lessons.objective: I can show that two expressions are equivalent by simplifying and combining like terms.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words equivalent, simplify, like terms, and combine.

concept.heading: When are two expressions equivalent?
concept.intro: Two expressions are equivalent when they always give the same value, no matter what number you put in for the variable. They can look different but mean the same thing.
concept.keyIdea: Equivalent Algebraic Expressions. 1. Equivalent expressions produce the same value for any substitution of the variable. 2. Simplify expressions using algebraic properties (Distributive, Commutative, Associative). 3. Test equivalence by substituting two different test numbers

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Producer A wrote 3x + 2x + 10 and Producer B wrote 5x + 10. Are they equivalent?
Both give 30, and 3x + 2x is just 5x, so they are equivalent.
linesEs: El productor A escribió 3x + 2x + 10 y el productor B escribió 5x + 10. ¿Son equivalentes?
Las dos dan 30, y 3x + 2x es justamente 5x, así que son equivalentes.

vocabulary.definition: Expressions that look different but have the same value for every allowed variable value.
vocabulary.example: 2(x + 3) and 2x + 6 are equivalent.

vocabulary.definition: Expressions that always have the same value.
vocabulary.example: 2x + 4 and 2(x + 2): when x = 3, both = 10; when x = 7, both = 18 — always the same

vocabulary.definition: To rewrite an expression in a shorter form that is still equal to the original.
vocabulary.example: 3x + 2x + 5 simplifies to 5x + 5 — fewer terms, same value

vocabulary.definition: Terms with the same letter raised to the same power, like 2x and 5x.
vocabulary.example: 3x and 7x are like terms (both x); 3x and 3y are NOT (x vs y); 3x and 3x² are NOT (x vs x²)

vocabulary.definition: To add or subtract terms with the same letter into one.
vocabulary.example: 4n + 3n = 7n — add the coefficients (4 + 3 = 7) and keep the variable (n)

vocabulary.definition: The number in front of a letter, like the 3 in 3x.
vocabulary.example: In 5x + 3, the coefficient of x is 5 — when x = 2, the 5x part equals 10

vocabulary.definition: The order of the numbers can change in addition or multiplication without changing the result.
vocabulary.example: a + b = b + a

vocabulary.definition: The grouping of the numbers can change in addition or multiplication without changing the result.
vocabulary.example: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c)

vocabulary.definition: One test value that shows two expressions are not equivalent.
vocabulary.example: One mismatch is enough.

title: Expression Remix Studio
mission: Translate a situation into an expression, substitute values, and test whether two expressions stay equivalent.
investigate: On paper, evaluate 4x + 3 when x = 5. Compare it with 4(x + 3) in the model. Why are the results different?
Compare a(x + b) with ax + ab for several values.
Explain why matching at only one value cannot prove two expressions equivalent.
create: Write a situation for an algebraic expression. Give an equivalent expression, justify it with a property, and verify both at two different values.

support.prompt: Which expression represents 'the product of 6 and a number n'?
support.explanation: 'Product' means multiplication, so the product of 6 and n is 6n.
feedback: 'Product' is the result of multiplication. 6 times n is 6n.
Adding 6 + n is not the same as 'the product of 6 and n'.
'Product' = multiply. 'Sum' = add. 6 and n multiplied is 6n.
hints: Underline the key word 'product.' Every operation has a code word — which operation does 'product' name?
Test with plain numbers: the product of 6 and 2 is 12. Which operation turned 6 and 2 into 12?
Use that same operation to join 6 and n. Writing a number right next to a variable shows it.

support.prompt: Which expression represents '9 less than a number y'?
support.explanation: 'Less than' means subtract from the number, so it's y − 9.
feedback: The order is flipped here. '9 less than y' starts at y and takes 9 away, so y has to come first in the subtraction.
This adds 9 instead of taking it away. The phrase 'less than' signals subtraction.
'Less than' flips the order: the number comes first, then subtract.
hints: 'Less than' is a tricky phrase — it flips the order of what you write.
Try it with numbers: '9 less than 20' means 20 − 9, not 9 − 20. Start with the amount you're taking from.
Copy the number pattern: '9 less than 20' → 20 − 9. Use the same order with y in place of 20.

support.prompt: Which expression represents 'the sum of a number m and 15'?
support.explanation: 'Sum' means addition, so the sum of m and 15 is m + 15.
feedback: That expression subtracts. 'Sum' is the word for the result of adding.
Writing a number right next to a variable means multiply. 'Sum' calls for a different operation.
Multiplying m and 15 would be 15m, not the sum.
hints: Circle the key word 'sum.' Which operation gives you a sum?
Check with numbers: the sum of 2 and 15 is 17. What did you do to 2 and 15 to get 17?
Take the operation that 'sum' names and place it between m and 15.

support.explanation: Substitute s = 10: 4.25 × 10 + 23.50. Multiply first: 42.50, then add: 42.50 + 23.50 = $66.00.
feedback: That adds 4.25 + 23.50 + 10 + 10 instead of substituting.
Check the multiplication: 4.25 × 10 = 42.50, not 43.25.
That adds before multiplying: (4.25 + 23.50) × 10.
hints: Replace s with 10.
Then add the one-time 23.50.

steps: Phrase: the product of a number n and 4
Reasoning: I saw two numbers and a variable, so I added them together.
support.explanation: 'Product' is a multiplication key word, so 'the product of a number n and 4' is 4n, not n + 4. Adding would match 'the sum of n and 4' — but 'product' tells you to multiply.
hints: Which operation does the key word 'product' name?
Test it: the product of 3 and 4 is 12, not 7.

feedback: Combine like terms: 4 + 3 = 7, so 4x + 3x = 7x.
4x and 3x are like terms. 4x + 3x = 7x.
Both have the same variable x. Add the coefficients: 4 + 3 = 7.
hints: 4x and 3x share the exact same variable, x — that makes them like terms.
Combine like terms by adding the coefficients (the number parts). The variable tags along unchanged.
Add the coefficients: 4 + 3. Keep the x exactly as it is — no new exponent appears.

feedback: You multiplied the 2 by the m but stopped there. The factor outside the parentheses has to reach every term inside.
2 times m is 2m, and 2 times 5 is 10.
Did you forget to distribute the 2 to both terms?
hints: The 2 outside the parentheses must multiply both the m and the 5.
Distribute: write 2 × m and 2 × 5, then join the products with +.
Start: 2 × m = 2m. Now multiply 2 × 5 and add that product on.

support.explanation: 5n + 2n = 7n. Add the coefficients: 5 + 2 = 7. The variable stays as n.
feedback: Combine: 5 + 2 = 7, so 5n + 2n = 7n.
5n and 2n are like terms. 5n + 2n = 7n.
Both terms have n. Add the coefficients: 5 + 2.
hints: 5n and 2n both have the variable n — they're like terms, so they can combine.
Add the number parts (coefficients) and keep n the same. Don't multiply them.
Compute 5 + 2 for the new coefficient, then write it in front of n.

steps: Distribute: Multiply the 3 by the first term only: 3 · x + 4
support.explanation: The 3 must multiply BOTH terms inside the parentheses, not just the first one: 3 · x + 3 · 4 = 3x + 12. Check x = 2: 3(2 + 4) = 18 and 3(2) + 12 = 18, but 3(2) + 4 = 10 — so 3x + 4 is wrong.
hints: How many terms are inside the parentheses? The 3 multiplies each one.
Substitute x = 2 into 3(x + 4) and into 3x + 4. Do you get the same value?

support.prompt: Predict the both expression values for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: 4(5 + 3) = 4×5 + 4×3 = 32. a(x + b) = ax + ab. Here a = 4, b = 3, x = 5. Distribution changes the form, not the value.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.
Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.explanation: The parentheses include both terms: 4 × (5 + 3) = 32. This is different from 4x + 3.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The expression 8n + 15 gives the cost of n tickets plus a fee. What is the cost for 6 tickets?
feedback: That adds 8 + 6 + 15 instead of multiplying.
That forgets the $15 fee.
That adds first: (8 + 15) × 6. Multiplication comes before addition.
hints: Replace n with 6.
Then add the fee.

steps: Phrase: 8 divided by a number m
Reasoning: I saw 'divided by' so I wrote the variable first and then 8.
core.explanation: '8 divided by a number m' means start with 8 and divide it by m: 8 ÷ m. Division is not commutative, so order matters — m ÷ 8 means something different (a number m divided by 8).
hints: What number comes first in '8 divided by m'?
Test it: 8 divided by 2 is 4, but 2 divided by 8 is 0.25 — order changes the answer.

steps: Combine: Combine every number you see: 7x + 2x + 3 = 9x + 3, then add the 9 and 3 too
core.explanation: Only LIKE terms combine. 7x and 2x are like terms (7x + 2x = 9x), but the 3 is a constant and cannot be added to the 9x. The simplified form is 9x + 3. Check x = 2: 7(2) + 3 + 2(2) = 21 and 9(2) + 3 = 21, but 12(2) = 24 — so 12x is wrong.
hints: Can you add 9x and 3 into one term? Are they like terms?
Substitute x = 2 into 7x + 3 + 2x and into 12x. Do you get the same value?

core.prompt: Predict the both expression values for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: 5(5 + 3) = 5×5 + 5×3 = 40. a(x + b) = ax + ab. Here a = 5, b = 3, x = 5. Distribution changes the form, not the value.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.
Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.explanation: The parentheses include both terms: 4 × (5 + 3) = 32. This is different from 4x + 3.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

steps: Phrase: 12 less than a number g
Reasoning: I see 'less than' so I subtract, and 12 comes first in the phrase.
stretch.explanation: '12 less than a number g' means start with g and subtract 12: g − 12. The phrase 'less than' reverses the order — the number being subtracted FROM comes after 'less than.'
hints: Does '12 less than g' mean start with 12 or start with g?
Try it with numbers: '5 less than 20' means 20 − 5 = 15, not 5 − 20.

stretch.prompt: Field day needs one $4.25 item per student plus a one-time $23.50 shipping fee. Write the expression, then find the cost for 30 students AND for 60 students. Does doubling the students double the cost? Explain.
stretch.explanation: The expression is 4.25s + 23.50. For s = 30: 4.25 × 30 + 23.50 = 127.50 + 23.50 = $151.00. For s = 60: 4.25 × 60 + 23.50 = 255.00 + 23.50 = $278.50. Doubling the students does NOT double the cost. Twice $151.00 would be $302.00, but the actual cost is $278.50 — a difference of exactly $23.50. The reason is that only the 4.25s term depends on the number of students; the shipping fee is a constant charged once no matter how many students come, so it is not doubled along with everything else.
hints: Write the per-student term and the one-time constant separately.
Substitute each value of s and evaluate.
Compare double the first cost to the second cost — what is the difference, and where does it come from?

stretch.explanation: 3x + 2x = 5x (NOT 5x²). When you combine like terms, you add the coefficients, not multiply them. The correct answer is 5x + 6.
hints: When you combine 3x + 2x, do you add the exponents or the coefficients?
3x means 3 groups of x. 2x means 2 groups of x. Together that's ___ groups of x.

stretch.prompt: A student says 2x + 3 and 5x are equivalent because both equal 5 when x = 1. Is the student correct? Explain why testing one value is not enough to prove equivalence, and find a value of x where they give different results.
stretch.frame: The student is ___ because ___. When x = 1: 2(1) + 3 = ___ and 5(1) = ___. But when x = ___: 2(___) + 3 = ___ and 5(___) = ___. To prove equivalence, expressions must be equal for ___ values of x.
stretch.explanation: The student is not correct. Both expressions really do equal 5 when x = 1, but equivalence means equal for EVERY value of x, and one lucky match proves nothing. Testing x = 2 gives 2(2) + 3 = 7 while 5(2) = 10 — that single counterexample settles it.
hints: Both expressions equal 5 at x = 1 — but equivalence means equal for EVERY value of x.
Hunt for a counterexample: pick another value, like x = 2, and evaluate both expressions.
Try x = 2: compute 2(2) + 3 and 5(2). If the results differ, you've proven they're not equivalent.
